method.standout: the published finding is the year that most exceeds the median of the +/-5 years around it, scored as excess over that baseline in units of its square root (floor 30 mentions, and at least 2.0x the neighbourhood). Years within 5 of the observed range's edges are not eligible, because beyond the inherited ceiling every year is structurally zero and the edge would always look surprising. Not the most-invoked year: that is the ceiling, not a finding. Not a plain ratio either: that crowns the thinnest neighbourhood.
method.inherited_ceiling: GDELT's extractor emits no year >= 2015 (measured as a clean cliff on 2026-08-14 and re-measured nightly as max_year_observed). The instrument's scope is the press's memory of 1800-2014; recent-decade invocation is not available from this field and is not substituted from another population.
method.why: beside the standout year the file publishes the evidence for it, all measured from the same rows: GDELT theme codes, extracted persons and organisations, the headlines of the invoking articles, and the anniversary arithmetic (the year's most-invoked exact date against the record's own date). The event is never named here — the receipts are shown and the naming is the reader's.

law_test.hypothesis: Candia et al. 2019, biexponential decay of collective attention
law_test.reason: the 20 tracked events are 12 to 145 years old and Candia's curve is a function of an item's age in years, while the 48 days since the register was founded have moved each of them by 0.13 of a year, so a fit to this series would read the news cycle, anniversaries and the register's own selection effect as decay; fitting one day's age profile instead stays rejected, because it mixes how many datable events each year produced with how fast they fade, and the extractor's inherited ceiling (no year >= 2015) removes the young ages where the curve's fast phase lives
